1.b: Norbert Wiener, the MIT mathematician whose significance is covered extensively on this timeline, published Cybernetics: or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine in 1948.

2.b: Digital creativity witnessed a revolution with the invention of Kid Pix. Developed by Craig Hickman and published by Broderbund Software in 1991, Kid Pix marked a paradigm shift in computer software designed for children. lerandom.

3.t: Xerox PARC Develops Alto Personal Computer
3.b: On the cutting edge, the Alto had a bitmapped screen and pioneered the graphics-based display, mouse, windows and icons that later systems inherited.

4.t: One Of Us Is Real And It’s Not You at Galerie Yeche Lange
4.b: Speaking of exciting New York digital-friendly galleries, hello, Galerie Yeche Lange.

5.t: Bauhaus Weaving Workshop Initiated by Gunta Stölzl
5.b: After Gunta Stölzl asked for a class for women to be set up, the weaving workshop was created by the women themselves and taught by Helena Börner.

6.b: Between 1989 and 1992, Stenger worked on Angels, the first immersive movie and an important early VR work. She developed the project at MIT and the University of Washington with an Advanced Visualizer. Users could interact in the space with a VPL Dataglove.

7.b: For further proof that our fear of producing intelligent machines that could one day overtake us is nothing new, see Samuel Butler's satirical novel Erewhon; or, Over the Range.

8.b: Knowlton, a pioneer of computer art and animation, at Bell Labs developed BEFLIX, the first general-purpose programming language for computer animation.BEFLIX is short for “Bell Flicks” and was written in macro FAP, the Fortran Assembly Program.

9.t: The Mathematical Basis of the Arts by Joseph Schillinger
9.b: This book, influential to later computer artists, promoted the concept that codified mathematical language could generate art when combined with a machine.

10.t: Ivan Moscovich Begins Experimenting with Mathematical Forms
10.b: Mathematician Ivan Moscovich experimented with different mechanisms to create complex curves and shapes based on mathematical formulas. His work demonstrated the potential of algorithmic processes to generate intricate and visually appealing designs.

11.t: Vera Molnár Begins her Iconic (Des)Ordres Series
11.b: One of Molnár’s most recognizable series of works, (Des)Ordres consists of a grid of concentric squares with random distortions that highlight the distinction between order and chaos.

12.t: Art After Modernism: Rethinking Representation, edited by Brian Wallis
12.b: This seminal book, comprised of twenty-five essays, explores the evolving landscape of contemporary art in the post-modern era, marking a critical shift in art discourse by examining the rejection of modernist principles and the emergence of new artistic paradigms.

13.t: Demoscene Splinters into PC and Home Computer
13.b: This year represents the beginning of the split in the demoscene community that would coalesce over the next several years, as some practitioners moved to the PC while others stayed on home computers such as the Commodore 64, Amiga and Atari ST.

14.t: Vibe Check: A Brave New World
14.b: You can sum up 2025 in two words: vibe coding. There. Timeline 2025 finished.But wait. That’s not all. The concept captures more than at first glance: the rise of AI agents, Opus 4.5, AI autonomy, new directions in art, new directions for humanity.

15.b: This New Tendencies magazine published by Zagreb City Galleries would release nine editions from 1968-1972.The Zagreb group would go on to organize the iconic Tendencies 4 in 1969. 1968 saw the release of “Bit No.

16.b: Formed by artists including Gyula Kosice, Carmelo Arden Quin, and Rhod Rothfuss, Madí embraced concrete art and sought to create a new visual language using abstract shapes and colors, considered an important part of the history of Concrete Art in Latin America.

17.b: This four-minute animation by Max pioneered the use of realistic, simulated water. It also featured weather effects. This work of realistic fluid simulation was instrumental in the development of computer-generated images for films, animation and art.

18.b: Manolo Gamboa Naon (aka Manoloide) began his Processing sketches in 2012, according to himself on his github page. Considered a prodigy for his extensive, high-quality ouput, Manolo’s work can be viewed—largely unminted—on his behance page.

19.b: This IRL Pac-Man Pac-Manhattan was an innovative work of urban-performance art that transformed the streets of New York City into a live-action videogame, replicating the classic 1980's arcade game Pac-Man.

20.b: Released shortly after Ethereum’s mainnet launch, Etheria, the first Ethereum NFTs, consisted of a plot of virtual land. While several years before NFTs became popular, Etheria was quite modestly known until the crypto bull run of 2021.

21.t: A-Volve by Christa Sommerer and Laurent Mignonneau
21.b: A-Volve (1993–94) was an interactive-evolutionary art environment that stands as an important step in the development of AI art. For the piece, visitors could draw virtual organisms using a sensor pencil, which then came to life in a water-filled glass pool.

22.t: Music and Connectionism, edited by Peter M. Todd and D. Gareth Loy
22.b: This book stands as a survey of the field of the creative application of neural networks to create music. The work expounds the early work of David Cope from 1981 and Todd’s own earlier ideas.

23.b: In another classic work of video game history, Velvet-Strike, by Anne-Marie Schleiner, Joan Leandre and Brody Condon, merged activism with video-game art as it was a protest against the newly launched Bush-era war on terrorism.

24.b: The SIGGRAPH ‘89 conference marked a watershed point in computer art history. A significant panel session evolved among the convergence of creative minds, provocatively titled “Computer Art—An Oxymoron?”

25.t: The Salon des Refusés Opens in Paris
25.b: The “exhibition of rejects,” a response to the rejection of many artists' works by the official Salon in Paris, begins. Since 1667, the Académie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture held public exhibitions for their standout students.

26.b: Some people are programmed to think differently, the people whose ideas change the paradigm. The field of AI lost one of those and one of its best too soon in 1971 when Frank Rosenblatt died in a boating accident in Chesapeake Bay.

27.t: Everydays: The First 5000 Days by Beeple
27.b: If two local catalysts propelled the NFT mania of 2021, they were the pandemic and this March 11 record-breaking Beeple sale.

28.t: Sonakinatography I Movement #III for Multi-Media by Channa Horwitz
28.b: Sonakinatography is the breakthrough series by Horwitz, meaning “sound,” “motion” and “notation.” On graph paper, she plotted the motion of eight entities over time with colors and numbers in 8x8 square grids.

29.b: The work we currently hold in high regard may shift in importance over time, while some notable contributions will inevitably be overlooked. Here is an ongoing list of standouts from the year.

30.t: International Computer Arts Festival at The Kitchen, New York
30.b: This festival featured panels, films, graphics and music made or inspired by computers. It included the work from a particularly impressive set of computer video pioneers such as William Fetter, Lillian Schwartz, Stan Vanderbeek and John Whitney.

31.b: This book chapter by one of the founders of computer art would have a significant impact on the development of 3D computer graphics in the coming decades.
